x: A body floats if it is less dense than the liquid, a hydrometer measures relative density, centrifugation lets denser particles settle, and ballast sets a ship's or submarine's average density, giving a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii.
t: Recall where density comparison is applied.

x: Option C is incorrect: a body floats when its density is less than the liquid's, not greater. The other statements on air density, centrifugation and hydrometers are true.
t: Check the direction of the density condition for floating.

x: Both are true and both show Pascal's law: hydraulic brakes pass pressure equally to all wheels, and a syringe passes pressure from one end to the other.
t: Recall Pascal's law: pressure on a confined fluid spreads equally.

x: Pressure rises with depth, so the bottom of a submerged body is pushed harder than its top. This pressure difference is the net upward buoyant force.
t: Recall that hydrostatic pressure increases with depth.

x: A ship floats when weight equals buoyant force, buoyancy keeps a swimmer afloat, a fish bladder adjusts buoyancy for depth, and hot air's lower density lifts a balloon, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall how buoyancy works in each case.

x: A water strider uses the surface as an elastic membrane, small drops are spherical to minimise area, surface tension holds up a needle, and soap bubbles have two surfaces with higher excess pressure, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall each surface-tension observation.

x: Both are true and R explains A: soaps and detergents lower water's surface tension, so it wets and penetrates dirt better and cleans more.
t: Check whether R is the mechanism behind A.

x: Water rises in a narrow tube with a concave meniscus, mercury is depressed with a convex one, water climbs through xylem, and blotting paper soaks ink through its pores, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Discriminate water (concave, rise) from mercury (convex, fall).

x: All four are capillary action: oil rising in a wick, damp rising in walls, water rising in plants and ink soaking into blotting paper.
t: Recall the everyday examples of capillarity.

x: All four are correct: viscous oils lubricate machines, streamlining cuts drag, viscosity affects blood flow, and raindrops and parachutes reach terminal velocity.
t: Recall the applications of viscosity.

x: Springs store and release elastic energy, rubber and tyres need a high elastic limit, crane cables use steel with high Young's modulus, and instruments use strings under tension, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the elastic property used in each application.

x: Submarine hulls need low-compressibility materials, sound speed depends on the medium's compressibility, pneumatic absorbers cushion with compressible air, and bulk modulus uses liquid incompressibility, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
t: Recall where compressibility matters.

x: All five use Archimedes' principle: ships, submarines, balloons and airships, hydrometers and lactometers, and life jackets.
t: Recall applications of buoyancy.

x: Buoyant force acts vertically upward through the centre of buoyancy, the centre of the displaced liquid. Weight acts downward through the centre of gravity.
t: Discriminate centre of buoyancy from centre of gravity.

x: Both are true: waterproofing raises the contact angle so water beads up, and the contact angle depends on surface tension.
t: Recall the link between contact angle and wetting.

x: All four are correct: water rises in plants by capillarity, lung surfactants lower surface tension, molten metal forms spheres in space, and droppers and pens rely on drop formation.
t: Recall the applications of surface tension.

x: A hydraulic jack lifts vehicles, excavators amplify force, a hydraulic press multiplies force, and hydraulic brakes pass pressure equally to all wheels, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall each Pascal's law device.

x: All three are correct: a hydrometer measures liquid density, a lactometer checks milk purity, and life jackets increase buoyant force.
t: Recall the applications of Archimedes' principle.

x: Mercury forms a convex meniscus and is depressed in a glass tube, because its cohesion is stronger than its adhesion to glass. Water does the opposite.
t: Discriminate mercury from water in a capillary.

x: Viscosity affects blood flow, hydraulic shock absorbers use viscous damping, paint and honey flow slowly, and raindrops reach terminal velocity, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall each viscosity application.

x: Bridges need strong elastic materials, instruments use strings under tension, rails need expansion gaps for thermal stress, and tyres need a high elastic limit, giving a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.
t: Recall the elastic property used in each structure.

x: All three are correct: liquids suit hydraulics because they barely compress, air's compressibility cushions pneumatic absorbers, and bulk modulus contrasts liquids with gases.
t: Recall compressibility of liquids versus gases.

x: Both are true: crane cables use steel with high Young's modulus, and molten metal forms spheres in space and in powder metallurgy because of surface tension.
t: Recall elasticity and surface tension applications.

x: Both are true and R explains A: ice is slightly less dense than water, so it floats, with only about a tenth above the surface.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Gases are highly compressible, so large amounts can be squeezed into cylinders. Liquids have low compressibility.
t: Discriminate gases (compressible) from liquids (incompressible).
